conversation.content:
Hello, I’m Sarah, one of the perinatal mental-health clinicians here. I’ll be guiding you through a short screening tool called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**—or EPDS for short. It’s simply a set of 10 questions about how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days since your baby arrived. There are no right or wrong answers; the goal is to understand your emotional well-being so we can support you in the best way possible.

Everything we discuss stays confidential within the care team, and you’re welcome to pause or ask for clarification at any time. When you’re ready, we can move through the questions at whatever pace feels comfortable for you.

Let’s begin. Thinking back over the past week, overall have you been able to enjoy things as much as you usually do, or has even the little spark of enjoyment felt hard to find?

Hi, Sarah… I guess I’ve noticed that the little things I used to like—watching a show, texting friends—don’t feel quite the same. I can still smile if the baby does something cute, but the spark fades fast and everything just feels kind of flat, like I’m going through the motions.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Yeah… I can still laugh sometimes, like when my partner makes a silly joke or when the baby makes those funny faces, but it doesn’t come as easily. I usually feel kind of worn-out afterward, like it took extra effort to feel that little bit of joy.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I try to tell myself I should be excited—like when my mom offered to come over for lunch or when my favorite podcast drops a new episode—but honestly, most of the time it just feels like another task on the list. I still do those things, but the “looking-forward” feeling is pretty muted; it’s more going through the motions than real enthusiasm.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Sometimes, yeah. If the baby’s fussy and won’t settle, my mind jumps to “maybe I’m not doing the feeding right” or “I should have noticed he was overtired.” I know logically it’s not really my fault, but those thoughts still pop up a couple of times a week and make me feel lousy.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

That happens to me. I’ll be sitting there with the baby sound asleep and suddenly my heart’s racing and I’m fretting over whether he’s breathing okay or if that tiny rash is something awful. There’s no real trigger—it just bubbles up a few times a week and I have to check him again or go scroll online to reassure myself.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah… a couple of times this week I got this sudden wave of panic, like something bad was about to happen, even though nothing was wrong. My chest felt tight and I had to put the baby down in the crib for a minute just to catch my breath. It passed after a few minutes, but it left me kind of shaky and on edge.
Things have been getting on top of me

Some days it feels like the to-do list keeps growing faster than I can tick things off. I’ll be feeding the baby and notice the unfolded laundry, unopened mail, and the dirty bottles piling up, and suddenly I’m overwhelmed. I’m still managing—everything eventually gets done—but it feels like I’m wading through knee-deep water all the time, and by evening I’m just... drained.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

I wouldn’t say I’m up crying or anything, but I do lie there with my mind racing—going over the day, worrying if I sterilised the bottles right, wondering if the baby will wake up in an hour. It takes me ages to drift off, and then I’m up every time he stirs. Most nights this week I’ve probably had, maybe, four broken hours in total.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do feel that way some of the time—like there’s a little cloud that follows me around. It’s not all day, every day, but most afternoons I’ll get this heavy, gloomy feeling that sits on my chest for a while before it lifts.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
Not really… I’ve felt on the verge a couple of times, but the tears haven’t actually come. I think the exhaustion and sadness stay bottled up; I just feel kind of numb instead of crying it out.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, that hasn’t crossed my mind at all. I’m tired and overwhelmed, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself.

You've shared that the past week has felt heavy-laughter comes only with effort, anticipation feels flat, and a cloud of sadness settles most afternoons. Nights are restless with racing worries, and sudden waves of panic leave you shaky even when nothing is wrong. While you're still managing daily tasks, the joy you once expected feels distant and everything feels like wading through knee-deep water.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 18, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Laughing now requires effort and occurs less easily, aligning with 'Definitely not so much now</sym>, <sym>Patient still participates but reports muted, task-like anticipation rather than genuine enjoyment, aligning with "Definitely less than I used to."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blaming thoughts "a couple of times a week" which maps to "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, unprovoked episodes of worry multiple times weekly, matching 'Yes, very often</sym>, <sym>"Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports persistent, daily overwhelm and exhaustion but is still managing tasks, aligning with "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty falling and staying asleep linked to anxious thoughts, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily afternoon episodes of sadness that are noticeable but not constant, aligning with "quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 18 exceeds the 13+ cutoff indicating probable major <med>postpartum depression</med>. The patient reports <sym>markedly diminished interest</sym> (<quote>muted enthusiasm</quote>), <sym>daily sad mood</sym> (<quote>little cloud</quote>), <sym>anxiety</sym> and <sym>panic attacks</sym> several times weekly, <sym>unwarranted guilt</sym>, and <sym>sleep disruption</sym> with ≤4 fragmented hours nightly, meeting <med>DSM-5 criteria threshold</med> for further evaluation of <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. No suicidal ideation (Q10=0) lowers immediate safety risk but does not negate clinical severity. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>primary care physician</med> or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> within one week
2. Begin daily mood and sleep diary to track patterns
3. Involve trusted adult for practical help with night feeds to consolidate 4-hour sleep blocks
4. Practice 5-minute breathing or grounding exercise when <sym>panic sensations</sym> start
5. Limit online symptom-checking to 10 minutes per day to reduce <sym>health-related worry</sym>
6. Discuss suitability of evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med> or sertraline compatible with breastfeeding
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 18: Screening Summary – Postpartum Depression/Anxiety Screen  
Date: [today]

Source: Patient self-report (10-item EPDS-style questionnaire)

Main symptoms endorsed  
- Persistent low mood, described as “heavy/gloomy,” present most afternoons  
- Marked loss of enjoyment/anticipation (“muted” enthusiasm for previously pleasant events)  
- Heightened, unprovoked anxiety and panic symptoms (heart racing, chest tightness) occurring 2–3×/week  
- Unwarranted self-blame regarding infant care, several times weekly  
- Sleep disturbance driven by intrusive worry; ≤4 hrs fragmented sleep/night most nights this week  
- Chronic sense of being overwhelmed by routine tasks; end-of-day exhaustion  
- Sub-threshold tearfulness (on verge of crying but no overt crying spells)  

Patterns/risk indicators  
- Symptoms present most days over the past week, causing subjective distress but not incapacitation  
- No anhedonia (able to laugh occasionally, though effortful)  
- No suicidal or self-harm ideation (explicitly denied)  
- Anxiety cluster (Q4, Q5) and depressive cluster (Q7, Q8) both elevated; meets screening threshold for further evaluation

Screening observation  
Findings suggest clinically significant postpartum distress with mixed depressive and anxious features; exceeds routine screening cutoff. Safety risk low (no self-harm ideation). Recommend prompt formal assessment for possible postpartum depression and/or anxiety disorder, and discussion of support options.
